chapter: Learning from Fletcher's circle in New York
title: How the Hawkins jam sessions worked: standards and stock arrangements
summary: Players call standards like Basin Street and Stardust; Horace takes four-bar intros, tunes run 20 minutes, then the group discusses what happened. They did it to learn each other's styles.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: This was back then -- when the stocks -- well they were just coming out. I got all those things downstairs now, you know. Like 'Limehouse Blues,' during that era and all those things. So these guys would call out these things -- 'Basin Street,' 'Stardust,' and all these things, you know. And I wouldn't know them, you know, but I could read, you know, the chords and everything else. So they would call out a tune and I say, 'Wait a minute, wait a minute.' Fletcher always kept his book in order, (inaudible), and they'd tell me to take a four-bar introduction, and I say, 'What do you mean?' And I'd do it a couple of times and then Hawk would take a four bar (inaudible). One tune would last sometime 20, 25 minutes, or longer, you know. Guys take different choruses, you know. Then when we finished that, we would stop like we'd recorded something -- stop and discuss what had transpired during that session, you know, that particular tune. And, man, that was a lesson. Those things don't happen any
more now like this, and they was regular sessions, and I used to ask some time why -- I say, 'You guys are too good to do these things. Why do you do it?' They say, 'Well, a lot of reasons.'

'We want to be familiar with each other's styles,' so this was the answer -- how to blend more together then, see. Even in those days, as quick as they were, they were never satisfied. They were always wanting to reach -- as you know in music is never conquered.
